The Cape Papers and Tristan da Cunha

The new South African government has received the Cape offices and their papers. Among them are the records linking Tristan da Cunha to the southern ports. Ministers enter that inherited claim in the national registers and authorise a future approach to the island's administration. The islanders' existing homes, livelihoods and customs must be respected in any settlement.
Propose a Convention for Tristan da Cunha

The British garrison sent from the Cape in 1816 secured the island for the Crown. Families on Tristan have since maintained close ties with the southern ports, even as passing ships have grown scarce. Our ministers would place the island under a South African administration while safeguarding the homes and customs of its inhabitants.

The surveyors have returned with charts and a plan for supplying the island. Where the shore remains outside any foreign administration, the government can send a landing party and establish its own outpost. The commissioners will organise the service from the Cape and record the undertaking in the national registers.

Families on Tristan have since maintained close ties with the southern ports, even as passing ships have grown scarce. A delegation from the victorious Boer government asks us to relinquish the island through a formal convention. Its ministers offer assurances concerning existing rights and visiting vessels. We may consent, propose negotiated terms or retain our administration.
The Commissioners for Tristan da Cunha

The island commissioners have received their instructions and registered the new administration. The Cape offices will arrange supplies and visiting vessels, while the ministry answers for the undertaking abroad. Existing rights are to be entered in the commissioners' books and respected by those who serve there.
Terms for the Tristan da Cunha Convention

Our delegation has returned with proposed terms. The present administration will consent to a transfer in return for an agreed settlement of its interests. Ratification would authorise the commissioners to receive the island and preserve the rights covered by the convention. Ministers may instead decline the terms and bring this mission to an end.
The Tristan da Cunha Proposal Is Declined

The delegation reports that the island's administration will not consent to our proposal. The ministry can reserve its diplomatic position or close the question in the interest of peaceful relations. The commissioners will return to the Cape, carrying the correspondence for the national archives.
Charts of Tristan da Cunha

The marine office has received the expedition's charts and observations. The report describes the landing places, the prevailing weather and the difficulties of keeping a station supplied. Ministers may now consider an outpost where the island remains outside a foreign administration, or pursue a convention with its present owner.
The Tristan da Cunha Mission Is Overtaken

Changed circumstances have overtaken the island mission. Its original mandate can no longer be executed on the terms under which the delegation was sent. The ministry recalls the commissioners and closes the correspondence, leaving the present administration to settle its affairs.
